passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

passages.text: To address this question, we introduce BMuon, which reweights Muon’s spectral geometry under a single global budget K K shared across all hidden channels of all MLP blocks. For hidden channel j j in block ℓ \ell , BMuon assigns an allocation μ j ℓ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \mu_{j}^{\ell}\in[0,1] to the corresponding row of the up-projection matrix and column of the down-projection matrix, with ∑ ℓ , j μ j ℓ = K \sum_{\ell,j}\mu_{j}^{\ell}=K . For a fixed allocation, BMuon introduces a diagonal reweighting inside Muon’s spectral-norm constraint, with the components of the update variable corresponding to channel j j in block ℓ \ell weighted according to its allocation μ j ℓ \mu_{j}^{\ell} . BMuon chooses the allocation globally, intuitively asking where the update budget should be spent to obtain the greatest first-order decrease in the loss.

NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

matches.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. matches.abstract_excerpt: We present a generic actor-critic method that combines a ridge-regularized pathwise least-squares temporal-difference (LSTD) critic with importance-corrected momentum (ICM) actors. matches.title: Learn the Directions, Normalize the Gains: Post-Training Normalization for LoRA
matches.abstract_excerpt: While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient task specialization, its learned updates can compromise capabilities beyond the target task. We identify \textbf{adaptation imbalance}: a few singular directions dominate the trained update, leaving its performance sensitive to how gains are allocated. We argue that \textbf{learning where to adapt does not ensure that adaptation gains are well balanced}. This motivates \textbf{LoRA-Norm}, a post-training normalization method that retains learned directions while rebalancing their gains. matches.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
matches.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

A practitioner fine-tuning a pretrained backbone on a few thousand possibly mislabeled examples has a capacity dial to set, the rank r r of low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , and double descent tells them which way to turn it. As capacity grows, test risk follows the classical U-shape, peaks near the interpolation threshold where the model first fits the training data exactly, and then descends again, so that the largest interpolating models often generalize best ( Belkin et al., 2019 ; Nakkiran et al., 2020 ; Spigler et al., 2019 ) . Label noise, the very condition that makes rank selection worth worrying about, amplifies the peak ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) . Applied to the rank axis, the advice is counterintuitive and actionable: once past the peak, raise the rank. Whether the rank axis obeys that advice has not been measured. Prior work documents task-dependent rank optima, degradation at high rank, reduced memorization under low-rank updates, and theoretical analyses of rank ( Jung et al., 2025 ; Rathore et al., 2025 ; Steele, 2026 ; Park, 2026 ; Zindari et al., 2026 ; Bossy et al., 2026 ) , and double descent has been analyzed in linear and deep transfer learning ( Dar & Baraniuk, 2022 ; Dar et al., 2022 ) . None combines an operational interpolation threshold on the rank axis, risk measurements past the expressivity limit r = d r{=}d (the model width, at which the adapter can first express any dense update), and a comparison of the tail with the same modules trained densely. The sweep range and the dense reference decide the answer.

The shape, and where sweeps stop. Sweeping rank on an ImageNet-pretrained DeiT-Tiny under label noise, we find test risk minimized at r = 1 r{=}1 , climbing steeply exactly as ranks acquire the ability to fit the noisy labels, and peaking well below full rank. We call this shape the interpolation cliff (Figure 1 ). What matters for measuring the axis is where sweeps conventionally end. Stopped at full rank, the axis has undone 0.033 0.033 of the 0.531 0.531 nats the peak cost and reads as a flat plateau. When the sweep extends to 4 ​ d 4d , risk keeps descending. Whether a sweep sees the second descent depends on how far it is allowed to run (Section 3 ). Figure 1: Two shapes, and why the reference point decides between them. (a) On a from-scratch capacity axis, risk peaks at interpolation and then descends past its own pre-peak valley, the only reference such an axis has. (b) On an adapter’s rank axis a second reference exists, dense fine-tuning of the same modules. Parity, the rank at which the adapter has as many trainable weights as dense fine-tuning, arrives before r = d r{=}d , the smallest rank that can express every dense update, so the adapter stops saving parameters before it is as expressive as dense. Schematic; measurements in Figure 2 .

A protocol that sets the reference point. “How much of the peak was undone” has no answer without a reference, and this axis offers two that disagree. Grading the tail against the sweep’s own valley is what the double-descent literature does, because a from-scratch width sweep has no unrestricted counterpart to compare against. An adapter axis has one. The module-matched rank sweep (MMRS) runs the dial past full rank and grades every point against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules, sharing seeds, subsets and noise draws, with the trainable-parameter ratio reported beside every risk difference (Section 4 ). On this family the two references have room to disagree, because the window in which the adapter saves parameters closes at parity, r = 0.75 ​ d r{=}0.75d , before it can express every dense update at r = d r{=}d (Figure 1 b).

What the tail costs. Under MMRS the descent is real and its price is legible. Every measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters has higher test negative log-likelihood (NLL) than dense, in every seed at a shared learning rate, so the descent becomes competitive with dense only after the adapter has stopped being cheaper than what it replaces. DeiT-Tiny first meets an equivalence margin of 0.05 0.05 nats at r = 3 ​ d r{=}3d , four times dense’s projection-weight count, and that result rests on one shared learning rate. The cheap end is a different matter: r = 1 r{=}1 leads dense by 0.40 0.40 and 0.27 0.27 nats on DeiT-Tiny and ViT-Tiny using 0.007 × 0.007\times dense’s projection-weight count, by far the largest risk reduction per added parameter. Qwen2.5-7B remains above dense at every measured rank while falling below its own pre-peak valley, so the two references answer the same sweep differently (Section 5.3 ). Since full rank supplies the expressivity, the remaining gap is not a function-class deficit; freezing one factor and controlling its spectrum isolates a condition-number effect on risk that disappears when the optimizer operates in update space (Section 5.4 ).

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Fine-tuning changes the behavior of a pretrained model by writing an update relative to what that model already knows. How many bits are actually required to preserve this acquired behavior? Parameter count, adapter rank, and numerical precision measure storage, but need not measure the information that matters functionally. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides a clean setting for studying this question: the base model remains frozen while the learned update is isolated in a separate adapter that can be compressed after training. We take a receiver-relative rate–distortion view of this process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , fine-tuning acts as an encoder, the adapter as a finite-rate message, and the frozen model as side information available when that message is decoded. We measure rate by the exact serialized size of a compressed adapter and distortion by the behavior of the resulting composed model. For a fixed retention target, the behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} is the smallest measured rate that preserves the required fraction of the held-out fine-tuning gain. This operational definition exposes a gap between numerical and behavioral compression. Lower weight reconstruction error need not preserve more learned behavior, and comparable bit budgets can have different effects depending on where compression acts. Behavioral rate also increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budget. Most importantly, the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers. A correction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. Compression can also reveal structure

ction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. Compression can also reveal structure within a learned update. Under deliberately corrupted reasoning supervision, fine-tuning can strongly damage the frozen model, yet aggressive compression recovers much of the lost performance and can exceed the frozen baseline. On Qwen2.5-7B, for example, GSM8K accuracy falls from 77.6% to 23.7% after corrupted fine-tuning and returns to 82.9% after compression. Singular-direction analyses show that harmful and useful effects are distributed unevenly across the update, while matched-norm controls show that the recovery is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. Finally, once an update has been trained, its behavioral rate closely tracks how far it can be shrunk before losing its gain. A simple codec-specific rule, R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) ≈ α 90 / γ R^{\star}(0.90)\approx\alpha_{90}/\gamma , achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value on 42 checkpoints from five receivers not used to fix the rule, although the evaluation remains retrospective. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning is not an intrinsic property of the data or of parameter displacement alone: it depends on the frozen receiver, the behavior to preserve, and how the learned corrections are represented within the update.

The previous analysis asks what can be inferred before the update is trained. Once the learned update is available, a simpler relationship emerges. Section 5 showed that aggressive compression often acts behaviorally like shrinking the update, although it is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. This suggests that compression difficulty may depend on how far the learned update can be reduced before its acquired behavior is lost. decision.reason: NormPre directly fits spectral optimization and LLM pretraining, but its abstract is truncated. Measured gains, memory, and throughput against Muon and AdamW could change whether it earns one of the ten slots. The BMuon disagreement is resolved by inspection: it addresses compressibility but targets channel pruning and trades off dense-model quality.
decision.question: In GPT-2, LLaMA, and Qwen3 pretraining, what validation loss or perplexity, peak training memory, and throughput do NormPre-G and NormPre-L achieve versus Muon and AdamW at matched tokens or compute? What are the model sizes and experimental controls?

result.question: In GPT-2, LLaMA, and Qwen3 pretraining, what validation loss or perplexity, peak training memory, and throughput do NormPre-G and NormPre-L achieve versus Muon and AdamW at matched tokens or compute? What are the model sizes and experimental controls?

passages.text: Experimental Setup. We evaluate NormPre across model scales, architectures and datasets. Our experiments cover GPT-2 Small on OpenWebText ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019 ) , LLaMA-{130M, 350M, 1.3B} on C4 ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Raffel et al., 2020 ) , and Qwen3-{0.6B, 1.7B} on Pile ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2020 ) . We compare NormPre-G and NormPre-L with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and MANO ( Gu and Xie, 2026 ) . NormPre-G uses five Newton-Schulz iterations and NormPre-L uses the Sketch implementation with rank r = 32 r=32 . All models are trained for 10,000 10{,}000 steps with a sequence length of 1024 1024 and an effective batch size of 512 512 . Within each setting, all optimizers use matched model initialization, data order, training budget and evaluation protocol. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix A.1 . Table 1: Validation loss across model scales, architectures and pretraining datasets. GPT-2 Small results show mean ± \pm standard deviation over three matched seeds, and larger models report single-run results under matched training budgets. Shaded columns indicate our variants. The best baseline and our outperforming variants are shown in underline and bold , respectively. Figure 1a shows training and validation loss trajectories averaged over three matched seeds. Both variants achieve lower training and validation loss than the baselines during later training, demonstrating the effectiveness of NormPre. Table 1 confirms that both variants outperform all three baselines in mean best validation loss, with NormPre-G achieving the lowest value. Compared with the strongest baseline Muon, NormPre-G and NormPre-L reduce validation loss by 0.0397 0.0397 and 0.0238 0.0238 , respectively.

LLaMA Pretraining on C4 and Qwen3 Pretraining on Pile. We extend the comparison to LLaMA-{130M, 350M, 1.3B} on C4 and Qwen3-{0.6B, 1.7B} on Pile. Table 1 and Figures 1b – 1d show that both variants consistently outperform all three baselines across these diverse architectures, with NormPre-G achieving the lowest loss. For LLaMA, the advantages over the strongest baseline are most pronounced at the largest evaluated scale (1.3B), where NormPre-G and NormPre-L reduce validation loss by 0.0392 0.0392 and 0.0301 0.0301 , respectively. These optimization gains extend similarly to Qwen3. Notably, NormPre-L performs closely to NormPre-G at the 1.7B scale with a minimal loss difference of 0.0029 0.0029 (Qwen3 loss curves are deferred to Appendix A.2 ).

Training. All models are trained for 10,000 10{,}000 optimization steps with sequence length 1024 1024 and effective batch size 512 512 . We use linear warmup followed by cosine decay to 10 % 10\% of the peak learning rate, with the model-specific learning rates and warmup steps given in Table 3 . Weight decay is 0.1 0.1 and gradients are clipped at 1.0 1.0 . All models are evaluated every 500 500 optimization steps. GPT-2 Small uses 200 200 randomly sampled validation mini-batches per evaluation, while LLaMA and Qwen3 evaluate on the complete fixed validation split of 2,048 2{,}048 sequences. Within each setting, all compared optimizers use matched model initialization, data order, training budget, base learning-rate schedule and validation protocol. All experiments use the same PyTorch training codebase and NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. GPT-2 Small uses one GPU per training trajectory and LLaMA and Qwen3 use four-rank data parallelism.

Training and Validation Loss for Qwen3 Models. We provide the training and validation loss curves for Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B on Pile in Figure 5 . (a) Qwen3-0.6B on Pile (b) Qwen3-1.7B on Pile Figure 5: Qwen3 Models on Pile. Training and validation loss for Qwen3-{0.6B, 1.7B} with AdamW, Muon, MANO, NormPre-G and NormPre-L. For training loss, dark curves denote 50-step moving averages and light curves the raw trajectories. Training Efficiency Configurations. Efficiency measurements mirror the main pretraining configurations (including model architecture, sequence length of 1024, effective batch size of 512, and gradient clipping) with the following specific profiling protocols: • Precision & Data Loading: GPT-2 Small and LLaMA use FP32 parameters with BF16 autocast, while Qwen3 uses pure BF16. OpenWebText is fully materialized in host memory, whereas C4 and Pile are read dynamically from persistent NumPy memmaps (transferring only the active batch to the GPU to avoid full-dataset materialization). • Measurement Window: We profile 100 optimizer steps following 20 warmup steps. To isolate core algorithmic overhead, we disable optimizer diagnostics (e.g., descent alignment), validation, checkpointing, W&B logging, and torch.compile . • Metric Definitions: Optimizer latency isolates optimizer.step() using strict CUDA synchronization immediately before and after the call. E2E step time encompasses the complete training loop (data transfer, forward/backward passes, gradient accumulation, clipping, and optimizer update). Throughput is computed as global tokens per E2E step time, and peak memory tracks the maximum CUDA allocated memory during a measured step.

• TF32 Settings: Unless otherwise stated, TF32 refers to the CUDA matrix-multiplication TF32 setting. To isolate intrinsic algorithmic scaling from hardware-specific Tensor Core accelerations at small dimensions, the main GPT-2 Small efficiency results disable TF32. Training Efficiency on Qwen3-1.7B. We further evaluate training efficiency on Qwen3-1.7B with Pile under the main experimental configuration. Similar to the observations in Section 4.2 , relative to Muon, NormPre-G increases optimizer latency by 6.77 % 6.77\% , with an end-to-end step-time overhead of 0.53 % 0.53\% . NormPre-L reduces optimizer latency by 57.16 % 57.16\% , yielding a 4.21 % 4.21\% reduction in step time and a 4.41 % 4.41\% increase in throughput. Both variants remain slower per step than AdamW and MANO. All evaluated optimizers have the same whole-training peak allocated memory of 53.17 53.17 GiB per GPU. This shared peak is determined by forward and backward computation, whose memory peak exceeds that of the optimizer step. Table 5: Training Efficiency on Qwen3-1.7B. Measurements use the same training configuration as the main Qwen3-1.7B experiment and are averaged over 100 optimizer steps after 20 warmup steps. We report global throughput across 4 GPUs and per-GPU peak allocated memory. passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. This allows us to explore what characteristics of matrix optimizers lead to richer learning.

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

We first evaluate whether increasing adapter effective rank mitigates the learning–forgetting trade-off in a heterogeneous supervised fine-tuning setting that proxies continual learning. We report the Roy–Vetterli effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) of the accumulated update (higher indicates fuller use of available adapter capacity), training-mixture perplexity (Train PPL), and perplexity on the retention probes described above. This reported diagnostic differs from the Rényi-2 surrogate optimized by the penalty. Lower perplexity is better throughout. Figure 2 summarizes all methods across adapter capacity (panel A) and the learning–forgetting trade-off (panels B–D). The favorable region in the trade-off panels is the lower-left corner (strong learning with limited forgetting). Appendix Table 5 reports the full numbers; entries with ± \pm are means and sample standard deviations over three training executions, except PiSSA ( n = 2 n=2 ), and the remaining rows are single runs. PiSSA excludes one resumed execution with apparent data replay (Appendix G.1 ); its small two-run SD does not establish low population variability.

Figure 2: Dense FT denotes dense down-projection fine-tuning. Mixed-domain continual-learning baselines on Qwen2.5-0.5B (base, not Instruct; rank r = 896 r{=}896 unless noted). Each point represents a method–penalty configuration; the legend maps dot colors to adapter type. Points show multi-run means or single-run endpoints; sample SDs are reported in Appendix Table 5 . (A) Effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) shown as a vertical strip from 0 0 to nominal rank 896 896 (horizontal dashed line), with horizontal offsets only for visibility; higher indicates fuller adapter capacity utilization. (B–D) Learning–forgetting trade-offs: Train PPL (mixture learning) versus Wiki PPL, StarCoder PPL (pretraining proxies), and WMT CS–EN PPL (in-mixture translation retention); lower-left is better. The three Rényi-2 penalty points use different regularization weights λ \lambda . Unpenalized PiSSA and LoRA-XS have the highest Wiki perplexities; VeRA, SVF, and TinyLoRA limit forgetting with weaker mixture fit. NB-LoRA approaches the λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 learning–retention trade-off. Unpenalized PiSSA uses two runs after excluding one resumed execution with apparent data replay; the other multi-run points use three executions. Dense FT, LoRA at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , and penalized PiSSA at λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 are single runs. Full numeric values and the PiSSA exclusion are documented in Appendix Table 5 and its accompanying text.

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient . Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. GDLoRA incorporates complementary normal gradients without increasing standard LoRA’s optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification show that GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the performance gap to FFT. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GDLoRA .

Although these adapter-based methods do not require periodic full-gradient SVD refreshes, their first-order weight-space updates remain restricted to directions accessible through the current LoRA parameterization. This motivates us to investigate gradient information beyond these accessible directions. Although the accessible space evolves as the factors change, gradient components orthogonal to it cannot be expressed through first-order factor perturbations at the current iterate. We therefore ask: Can we explicitly recover and exploit this complementary gradient information while retaining standard LoRA’s optimizer-state memory budget? To address this question, we characterize the LoRA-accessible gradient space , consisting of all equivalent weight-space gradients induced by the Euclidean factor gradients, and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient evaluated at the current model parameters. We call the component orthogonal to the accessible space the normal gradient . When nonzero, its negative provides a local descent direction for the current batch loss with the adapters and other weights held fixed. It is also orthogonal to every first-order weight-space direction available to the current adapters. These properties motivate using the normal component to supplement standard LoRA optimization.

Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient of LoRA-injected layers from forward activations and backward signals, normalizes the recovered gradient by the number of input positions, and extracts its normal component using the current LoRA tangent space. This additional token-count normalization applies only to the normal branch and preserves the gradient direction. The adapter parameters follow standard AdamW optimization, while the token-normalized normal gradient directly updates the base weights initialized from the pretrained model. Both branches use quantities computed from the same pre-update parameters. The normal branch introduces no additional momentum or variance buffers for the base weights. In this way, GDLoRA approaches or matches the performance of full fine-tuning in the evaluated settings, without introducing additional optimizer-state memory overhead relative to standard LoRA under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We characterize the LoRA-accessible gradient space through its equivalence to the tangent space induced by the current parameterization, and identify the normal gradient as a complementary component with a local descent interpretation. • We propose GDLoRA , which retains standard AdamW optimization of the LoRA factors and applies the token-normalized normal gradient directly to the base weights, without introducing additional base-weight momentum or variance buffers.

We compare GDLoRA with full fine-tuning (FFT), standard LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , Fira ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , and five LoRA variants: PiSSA ( Meng et al., 2024 ) , DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , rsLoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) , LoRA-GA ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and LoRA-Pro ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . FFT updates all model parameters during fine-tuning. The LoRA variants seek to narrow the performance gap between LoRA and FFT through improved initialization, weight parameterization, scaling, or optimization. During fine-tuning, their updates remain governed by their respective adapter parameterizations. Fira instead combines low-rank gradient projection with scaled residual updates to enable full-rank weight adaptation. GDLoRA supplements standard LoRA with normal-gradient updates applied directly to the base weights, extending adaptation beyond the first-order weight-space directions accessible through the current LoRA parameterization. passages.text: For much of modern deep learning, large scale optimization was dominated by SGD and Adam-like coordinate-wise methods, while matrix preconditioning and approximate curvature methods remained comparatively limited in practice. Their additional memory, numerical, and systems requirements made their advantages difficult to realize at scale ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ; Gupta et al., 2018 ) . This landscape is beginning to change. Recent foundation models with multi-billion and trillion parameters ( Team et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Khona et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) are effectively trained with spectral optimizers such as Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) at substantially large model, data, and batch scales. This empirical shift raises a theoretical question. The implicit bias analysis of gradient descent (GD) shows that Euclidean geometry slows the progress of weak singular modes and thereby promotes low-rank solutions in deep matrix factorization ( Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ) . Whereas spectral normalization and curvature correction are designed to reduce precisely this kind of anisotropy, in idealized limits they can weaken or even cancel the singular value dependent slowdown. Their recent success therefore raises the question of whether GD’s spectral bias induced by depth is lost, preserved in a weaker form, or replaced by a qualitatively different mechanism of mode selection. More broadly, we ask: When do modern optimizers merely accelerate a common learning trajectory, and when do they change which spectral components emerge, persist, or disappear?

We investigate these questions in deep linear networks, where depth changes the parameterization and optimization dynamics without changing the end-to-end linear functions. This makes it a particularly clean setting for separating optimizer-induced dynamics from parameterization-induced bias. Our theoretical analysis focuses on deep matrix factorization, a canonical special case in which the evolution of singular modes can be characterized explicitly. Specifically, in full observation regression, it exposes transient singular mode learning ( Saxe et al., 2013 ; Soudry et al., 2018 ) , while in underdetermined matrix sensing and completion, it permits direct study of which interpolating matrix is selected ( Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Rhee et al., 2026 ; Parviz et al., 2026 ) .

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

We first evaluate the optimizer dependent spectral dynamics in the full observation matrix factorization setting described in App. F , where the theoretical phase laws apply most directly. Figure 4: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning evaluation in matrix factorization. (a) Evolution of a weak target mode with μ = 0.18 \mu=0.18 , shown as the learned fraction σ ⁡ ( t ) / μ \sigma(t)/\mu . GD exhibits the factorization induced small mode barrier, whereas normalization and preconditioning substantially accelerate emergence. (b) Birth time to the common amplitude b = 0.03 b=0.03 as the target mode μ \mu varies. While ideal Muon is independent of the target mode ordering during birth, other optimizers are target sensitive. (c) Decay trajectories for an unsupported mode with target μ = 0 \mu=0 . Ideal Muon removes the mode in finite time, undamped K-FAC produces exponential decay, while GD, instantaneous Adam with fixed stabilization, and cumulative Shampoo retain increasingly slow tails near zero. Optimizer geometry therefore determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 6: Singular mode trajectories reveal optimizer dependent spectral clocks. GD exhibits strongly sequential learning;Adam reduces these delays, while Muon makes the modes evolve on nearly the same clock until they approach their respective targets. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

passages.text: Quantizing AdamW’s optimizer states reduces persistent storage, but quantization errors propagate through the moment recurrences and perturb subsequent adaptive updates. We redesign 4-bit optimizer-state quantization for AdamW from the perspective of rounding space : the coordinate in which a quantizer chooses between adjacent reconstruction levels. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean preconditioner error at the next step. A one-dimensional quadratic construction further shows qualitatively different optimization dynamics under state-space and preconditioner-space rounding. These results motivate Zero-Inclusive Preconditioner-space Stochastic Rounding ( ZIP-SR ), which retains zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space. As a complementary route, Zero-Excluding EDEN calibration ( ZE-EDEN ) uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook and rescales the quantized second-moment block to mitigate the preconditioner distortion caused by the positive quantization floor. Both configurations use 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) for the first moment, with targeted stochastic rounding of the LM-head first moment during the final 10% of training. Across GPT- and Llama-style pretraining experiments ranging from 130M to 2.7B parameters, both methods reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW’s mean validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size, with the largest reported gap reduction reaching 70% . In full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, both recipes achieve lower validation loss than TorchAO while remaining close to 32-bit AdamW on downstream tasks.

We pretrain GPT-style models at 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 2.7B parameters and Llama-style models at 130M, 350M, and 1.1B with three paired seeds. Table 4 reports absolute 32-bit AdamW validation loss and paired 4-bit gaps. Both methods reduce TorchAO’s mean gap at every model size. A single-seed GPT-style 834M experiment with cosine decay also finds lower gaps for ZE-EDEN and ZIP-SR than for TorchAO ( Section C.2 ). On GPT-style 2.7B, TorchAO undergoes a sharp late-cooldown divergence. At the validation checkpoint at 95% of training tokens, before the terminal regression its mean paired gap was + 0.0754 ​ ( 0.0034 ) +0.0754\,(0.0034) , compared with + 0.0471 ​ ( 0.0018 ) +0.0471\,(0.0018) for ZE-EDEN and + 0.0286 ​ ( 0.0024 ) +0.0286\,(0.0024) for ZIP-SR, where parentheses report sample SDs. Relative to TorchAO, these correspond to gap reductions of 37.6 % 37.6\% for ZE-EDEN and 62.1 % 62.1\% for ZIP-SR. Hence, both proposed optimizers were already closer to 32-bit AdamW before TorchAO’s terminal regression. Figure 7 , in the appendix, shows the GPT-style 2.7B validation loss trajectories. passages.text: Monarch–Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining Alexander Miasnikov 1 , Kabirov Ruslan 1 , Gleb Molodtsov 1 , Dmitrii Vlashchuk 1 , Vladimir Aletov 1 , Nail Bashirov 1 , Daniil Tikhonov 1,2 , Maxim Krutikov 1 , Aleksandr Shestakov 1,3,* , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1 1 BRAIn Lab 2 HSE University 3 MBZUAI * Work performed at BRAIn Lab prior to joining MBZUAI. Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

Figure 2 : MoE pretraining at the same token budget. Two-block Monarch–Muon reaches the reported final validation loss of dense AdamW with fewer active and total parameters. Holding the Monarch factorization fixed isolates the effect of the optimizer. We compare AdamW and Muon with two and four blocks, using the same token budget and training schedule within each architecture. Dense AdamW, dense Muon, and GaLore provide reference losses for the dense quality model. The MoE comparison retains the same routing architecture and changes only the selected projections and their optimizer. Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ). The two-block MoE reaches the reported loss of dense AdamW with 15% fewer active parameters and 25.4% fewer total parameters (767M versus 1.029B). Figure 2 places this endpoint in the training trajectory. Thus, matrix-aware updates remain useful when the optimizer acts on structured factors rather than dense weights. Increasing the block count further reduces storage, with a higher final loss under both optimizers. Dense Muon gives the lowest loss in each architecture, defining the quality reference for this representation tradeoff. The learned spectra provide a complementary view of the optimizer effect. At the same block count, Monarch–Muon retains a heavier singular-value tail than Monarch–AdamW in the gate and up projections (Figure 3 ). Similar patterns appear in additional layers and components (Appendix B ). Thus, the change in update geometry reaches the represented matrices, even though orthogonalization is local to their factors.

From the 834M reference onward, Monarch–Muon improves both full-step time and peak memory relative to dense Muon. The systems experiments measure training operations on larger reference architectures, separately from the complete quality runs in Appendix A.1 . Model-size headings give the dense reference counts. Monarch uses fewer trainable parameters at these reference widths. The timings measure the practical cost of each representation, including its forward, backward, and optimizer computations. Table 2 uses dense models of 257M, 834M, 1.4B, 3.5B and 6.89B parameters, Monarch–Muon with 4 blocks, microbatch 4 and random token batches, all on one NVIDIA H100 80GB. Step time is the median wall time of a full training step (forward, backward, optimizer step and gradient reset) after warmup; the optimizer step is timed separately. Peak memory is the maximum allocated memory during the step, and optimizer state is the memory of all optimizer buffers, including projection matrices. For GaLore, APOLLO, FRUGAL and Fira the projection is rebuilt every 200 steps; the rebuild is timed separately and excluded from the step time.

passages.text: Quantizing AdamW’s optimizer states reduces persistent storage, but quantization errors propagate through the moment recurrences and perturb subsequent adaptive updates. We redesign 4-bit optimizer-state quantization for AdamW from the perspective of rounding space : the coordinate in which a quantizer chooses between adjacent reconstruction levels. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean preconditioner error at the next step. A one-dimensional quadratic construction further shows qualitatively different optimization dynamics under state-space and preconditioner-space rounding. These results motivate Zero-Inclusive Preconditioner-space Stochastic Rounding ( ZIP-SR ), which retains zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space. As a complementary route, Zero-Excluding EDEN calibration ( ZE-EDEN ) uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook and rescales the quantized second-moment block to mitigate the preconditioner distortion caused by the positive quantization floor. Both configurations use 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) for the first moment, with targeted stochastic rounding of the LM-head first moment during the final 10% of training. Across GPT- and Llama-style pretraining experiments ranging from 130M to 2.7B parameters, both methods reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW’s mean validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size, with the largest reported gap reduction reaching 70% . In full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, both recipes achieve lower validation loss than TorchAO while remaining close to 32-bit AdamW on downstream tasks.

We now evaluate the complete optimizer configurations in Table 2 . The preceding controlled comparisons examine rounding space, EDEN calibration, and first-moment quantization separately; Section 5.1 first combines them into a single attribution at 834M, and the remaining experiments evaluate the complete configurations in pretraining and supervised fine-tuning. Both methods quantize the first moment with NF4, using RTN by default and switching the LM-head first moment to SR during the final 10% of training. These shared choices are combined with two second-moment designs: ZIP-SR applies Update-SR with the zero-inclusive Dyn4 codebook, whereas ZE-EDEN applies State-RTN with the zero-excluding Dyn4-NZ codebook and EDEN calibration. Full implementation and training details are given in Appendix B . Table 2: Optimizer-state configurations evaluated in the end-to-end experiments. ZIP-SR and ZE-EDEN share the NF4 first-moment design established in Section 4 , but use the two different second-moment quantization routes developed in Section 3 . The superscript ∗ \ast indicates a phase-dependent rule: the LM-head first-moment uses NF4-RTN before the final 10% of training and switches to NF4-SR only during that phase. Configuration First moment Second moment Non-LM-head LM-head Format Rule EDEN 32-bit FP32 FP32 FP32 — × \times TorchAO 4-bit SDyn4-RTN SDyn4-RTN Lin4-NZ State-RTN × \times ZIP-SR 4-bit NF4-RTN NF4-RTN/SR ∗ Dyn4 Update-SR × \times ZE-EDEN 4-bit NF4-RTN NF4-RTN/SR ∗ Dyn4-NZ State-RTN ✓ \checkmark

All three 4-bit configurations use packed 4-bit storage for eligible moment tensors and therefore have essentially the same persistent optimizer-state footprint. The codebook and rounding changes require no additional per-parameter state, and ZE-EDEN absorbs its calibration factor into the existing block scale. With block size 128 and one FP32 scale per block for each moment, storing both AdamW moments requires 1.0625 1.0625 bytes per parameter on eligible tensors, compared with 8 8 bytes per parameter for FP32 moment storage, corresponding to a 7.53 × 7.53\times compression. At the scale of our experiments, this corresponds to approximately 19.2 19.2 GB less persistent moment-state storage for the 2.7B-parameter pretraining model and roughly 21 21 – 56 56 GB less for the 3B–8B full-parameter SFT models. To keep the storage comparison controlled, all 4-bit methods use the same tensor-eligibility criterion as the TorchAO baseline. In our model configurations, only normalization-layer moment tensors fall outside this criterion and therefore remain in FP32.

The main pretraining and SFT comparisons use the configurations in Table 2 . For ZIP-SR and ZE-EDEN, the first moment uses NF4-RTN by default, with only the LM-head first moment switching to NF4-SR after 90 % 90\% of training. In the GPT-style 834M component comparisons, quantized first moments use RTN throughout training. The LM-head rule is therefore inactive in Tables 3 and 8 . We report absolute mean metrics for 32-bit AdamW and mean paired differences for the 4-bit methods. Each paired difference subtracts the matched 32-bit result for the same seed; parentheses denote sample standard deviations. Single-seed component results are identified separately.

passages.text: Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient of LoRA-injected layers from forward activations and backward signals, normalizes the recovered gradient by the number of input positions, and extracts its normal component using the current LoRA tangent space. This additional token-count normalization applies only to the normal branch and preserves the gradient direction. The adapter parameters follow standard AdamW optimization, while the token-normalized normal gradient directly updates the base weights initialized from the pretrained model. Both branches use quantities computed from the same pre-update parameters. The normal branch introduces no additional momentum or variance buffers for the base weights. In this way, GDLoRA approaches or matches the performance of full fine-tuning in the evaluated settings, without introducing additional optimizer-state memory overhead relative to standard LoRA under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We characterize the LoRA-accessible gradient space through its equivalence to the tangent space induced by the current parameterization, and identify the normal gradient as a complementary component with a local descent interpretation. • We propose GDLoRA , which retains standard AdamW optimization of the LoRA factors and applies the token-normalized normal gradient directly to the base weights, without introducing additional base-weight momentum or variance buffers.

(a) Gradient component ablation (b) Learning-rate sensitivity (c) Accuracy and memory Figure 2: Ablation studies and analysis of GDLoRA. (a) Comparison of gradient components on six GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-Base and RoBERTa-Large. (b) Sensitivity to the base-update learning rate when fine-tuning Llama-3-8B on Math10K.
