Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient of LoRA-injected layers from forward activations and backward signals, normalizes the recovered gradient by the number of input positions, and extracts its normal component using the current LoRA tangent space. This additional token-count normalization applies only to the normal branch and preserves the gradient direction. The adapter parameters follow standard AdamW optimization, while the token-normalized normal gradient directly updates the base weights initialized from the pretrained model. Both branches use quantities computed from the same pre-update parameters. The normal branch introduces no additional momentum or variance buffers for the base weights. In this way, GDLoRA approaches or matches the performance of full fine-tuning in the evaluated settings, without introducing additional optimizer-state memory overhead relative to standard LoRA under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We characterize the LoRA-accessible gradient space through its equivalence to the tangent space induced by the current parameterization, and identify the normal gradient as a complementary component with a local descent interpretation. • We propose GDLoRA , which retains standard AdamW optimization of the LoRA factors and applies the token-normalized normal gradient directly to the base weights, without introducing additional base-weight momentum or variance buffers.

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

We compare CORE with existing deep research harnesses on three benchmarks, and a component analysis examines the contributions of coarse-to-fine search and context management. We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

passages.section: Idea2Prior: Auditable Paper Retrieval and Ranking from Research Ideas
passages.text: Shitian Yang Ruijie Tao Jian Huang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Johns Hopkins University Affiliation: syang214@jh.edu , rtao12@jh.edu , jhuan243@jh.edu October 13, 2026

Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. For both optimizers, shaping temporarily raises validation loss while active, but the shaped runs overtake their baselines after its removal and finish lower. At 50k steps, it reduces Adam’s loss from 2.8824 2.8824 to 2.8435 2.8435 and SOAP’s from 2.8640 2.8640 to 2.8271 2.8271 , gains of 0.0389 0.0389 and 0.0369 0.0369 , respectively. decision.reason: The ten selections prioritize the profile’s central questions: spectral compressibility, low-rank and memory-efficient training, LoRA behavior, and one paper-retrieval system. I resolved the reviewers’ material disagreements by excluding BMuon because its language-model result trades substantially worse unpruned perplexity for channel-pruning robustness, and excluding the overlapping LoRA-geometry and matrix-factorization-only papers in favor of directly measured LLM results. Unresolved uncertainties that could change a practical ranking are independent reproducibility, full training-memory and runtime effects of 4-bit states, and GDLoRA’s reconstruction overhead; repeated inspection did not resolve the latter, and repository discovery would not establish correctness.

selections.summary: Spectral weight decay applies an additive singular-value correction. In 124M–500M LLaMA experiments, it lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss; the paper also reports clean-test gains under label noise.
selections.relevance: Direct match to spectral regularization, training for low-rank compressibility, and memorization under label noise.

evidence.quote: Across LLaMA models with $124$M to $500$M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss.
Regularization coefficients are calibrated in separate tuning runs using final clean-validation accuracy, independently at each noise level for MNIST and at 60 % 60\% noise for BERT.

selections.summary: Defines behavioral rate as compressed LoRA-adapter size needed to retain held-out fine-tuning gain. Rates vary across frozen base models; correction spectra rank rates within a receiver, and compression can recover performance after corrupted fine-tuning.
selections.relevance: Connects spectra, functional compressibility, LoRA, and noisy supervision.

evidence.quote: the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers.
On Qwen2.5-7B, for example, GSM8K accuracy falls from 77.6% to 23.7% after corrupted fine-tuning and returns to 82.9% after compression.

selections.summary: ORCA applies temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in LLM training, then releases it. The reported LLaMA, Qwen3, and MoE runs finish with lower validation loss than Muon, including a matched-target LLaMA 1.3B comparison at 60k versus 100k steps.
selections.relevance: Tests how spectral shaping changes training trajectories and quality across model scales.

evidence.quote: While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss.

The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain.

selections.summary: Ori tracks drifting low-rank gradient subspaces during LLM pretraining. At rank 32 on a 1B LLaMA C4 run, its reported perplexity is 29.14 versus 33.82 for GaLore and 19.92 for full-rank Adam; reported optimizer-state peak memory is 0.2487 GB versus GaLore’s 0.3385 GB.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses the quality, optimizer-memory, and speed tradeoffs of low-rank LLM training.

evidence.quote: at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB).

selections.summary: ZIP-SR and ZE-EDEN redesign 4-bit AdamW moment quantization. Across paired GPT- and Llama-style pretraining runs from 130M to 2.7B parameters, both reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW’s validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW; eligible persistent moments use 1.0625 rather than 8 bytes per parameter.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses optimizer-state compression and model-quality tradeoffs across scale.

evidence.quote: Both methods reduce TorchAO’s mean gap at every model size.

storing both AdamW moments requires 1.0625 1.0625 bytes per parameter on eligible tensors, compared with 8 8 bytes per parameter for FP32 moment storage, corresponding to a 7.53 × 7.53\times compression.

selections.summary: Monarch-Muon applies matrix-aware optimization to structured factors. At fixed structure it improves reported pretraining loss over Monarch-AdamW; separate 6.89B-reference systems measurements report 52.94 versus 68.87 GB peak memory against dense Muon.
selections.relevance: Useful for the quality, memory, and speed tradeoff of structured, matrix-optimized pretraining.

evidence.quote: Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ).

papers.summary: Defines behavioral rate as compressed LoRA-adapter size needed to retain held-out fine-tuning gain. Rates vary across frozen base models; correction spectra rank rates within a receiver, and compression can recover performance after corrupted fine-tuning.

evidence.quote: the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers.

papers.summary: ORCA applies temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in LLM training, then releases it. The reported LLaMA, Qwen3, and MoE runs finish with lower validation loss than Muon, including a matched-target LLaMA 1.3B comparison at 60k versus 100k steps.
papers.relevance: Tests how spectral shaping changes training trajectories and quality across model scales.

evidence.quote: While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss.

evidence.quote: at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB).

papers.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
